newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron pact will boost Israeli economy - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hebron pact will boost Israeli economy - analysts.

text.p: Israeli analysts and business executives on Thursday hailed the Hebron agreement, saying it would encourage foreign investors and thaw economic ties with the Arab world.
But they warned the accord would not jump-start Israel's slowing economy.

"The transition of Israel the pariah to Israel the continuer of the peace process, that should be a good sign for foreign investment and for tourism," said Jonathan Kolberg, president of Claridge Ltd, an investment company. "I'm feeling much better."

Israel and the Palestinian Authority on Wednesday signed the long-awaited accord that sets the terms for Israeli redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron and further withdrawals from the West Bank over the next 18 months.
Delays in redeployment from Hebron, which was originally scheduled to be implemented 10 months ago, had raised concerns among investors and business executives about the future of Middle East peace.
The peace process has been a crucial factor in luring foreign investors to Israel and in helping Israeli companies form strategic partnerships with overseas companies.
"It's pretty obvious that foreign investors will be much more keen on the Israeli economy and stock market in the wake of the agreement," said Eli Nahum of Zannex Securities.
"But the same is true for local investors," he said. "The business community and financial markets are great believers in the peace process and its benefits to Israel."
Analysts said, however, that the gains accruing to the economy and the markets should be kept in perspective.

"All our forecasts were based on the assumption that the peace process would continue," said Shauli Katznelson, chief eocnomist at Israel Discount Bank. "If there wasn't an agreement, it would have been a little worse; with one it will be a little better."
Discount is keeping to its forecast showing gross domestic product expanding by just 2.8 percent this year, compared with an estimated 4.4 percent in 1996 and 7.1 percent in 1995.
Katznelson said the important variables for the economy were the interest and exchange rates.
Nahum agreed. "As of yesterday, you can't ignore the peace process....But I always emphasize that peace alone cannot drive the market," he said.

Israeli stock prices moved higher on Wednesday but analysts attributed the rise to a number of factors, not only the Hebron accord. Share prices, Nahum noted, had been rallying since the strat of November, even as the Hebron talks were logjammed.
Israel's budding business ties with the Arab world and its tourism industry could be the two biggest beneficiaries.

Business with the Arab world had been slowly developing, but with the election of the hardline Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister last May and the delays in reaching an agreement on Hebron they nearly ground to a halt.

"A half year ago, before the elections, an Israeli businessman would visit Jordan and he would be introduced to friends, even Syrians and Iraqis. In the last six months that didn't happen," said Mandy Barak, head of the international division at the federation of Israeli Chambers of Commerce. "Perhaps we can return now to what was a half year ago."
"I hope now that the political situation has reached a period of stability," he said, saying that business should not be subject to ups and downs of political process

Barak said he was optimistic about developing relations with Jordan, Tunisia, Morocco, Qatar and Oman, but less so about Egypt. Businessmen have have been disappointed with Egypt until now and Barak said he doubted a Hebron deal would change things.
Israel's tourism industry, which is especially sensitive to political and security developments, is looking forward to renewed political stability.

The Tourism Ministry estimates tourist arrivals fell seven percent last year to 2.3 million. Avi Rosental, director of the Israel Hotel Association, attributed the drop to the rash of bus bombings in February and March, followed by Israeli strikes into Lebanon and the violence in September following the opening of the Temple Mount tunnel.
"We feel the Hebron agreement will give back to Israel and the region a sense of stability and security and will be a boost for tourism," said Rosental.
"This (agreement) will bring us back to the 10 percent growth rate of the previous five years," Rosental said.
